paragraphs: AnomSeer addresses a weakness in using multimodal language models to detect unusual time-series behavior: recognizing a broad pattern is easier than explaining exactly which structural details make it abnormal. The framework combines deciding whether an anomaly exists, locating it, and explaining the decision within one approach.

Training uses expert reasoning traces built from classical analyses, including statistical measurements and frequency transforms. These provide detailed signals that can be checked against the series. Its optimization method, TimerPO, adds an optimal-transport-based learning signal tied to time-series structure. It also uses an orthogonal projection designed to prevent that auxiliary signal from interfering with the main detection objective.

Across the evaluated anomaly scenarios, AnomSeer models built on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B-Instruct outperform larger commercial baselines in classification and localization accuracy, particularly for point and frequency anomalies. The models also produce plausible supporting explanations. These results connect more detailed structural supervision with better detection, while the stated plausibility of the explanations does not establish that every generated reasoning trace is correct.
icml-2026-anomseer-reinforcing-multimoda.tldr: AnomSeer trains multimodal models with structural time-series reasoning signals to improve anomaly classification, localization, and supporting explanations.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can perform well on ordinary images while remaining vulnerable to adversarial examples. Adversarial training is a common defense, but its theoretical basis for these models has been less developed. This paper studies simplified Vision Transformer architectures to explain when fitting adversarially perturbed training examples can also support reliable performance on unseen examples.

The central result is conditional: under a specified signal-to-noise requirement, a moderate perturbation budget, and particular regimes, adversarial training yields nearly zero robust training loss and robust generalization error. This permits benign overfitting, where fitting the training data very closely coexists with strong generalization. The analysis extends this phenomenon to adversarially trained Vision Transformers, beyond its earlier observation in adversarially trained convolutional networks.

Experiments with synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical findings. The contribution is an explanation of how overfitting and robustness can coexist under the studied conditions. Its guarantees concern simplified architectures and the stated regimes, so the result should be read as a conditional account of robust learning rather than a guarantee for every Vision Transformer.
icml-2026-benign-overfitting-in-adversar.tldr: Under specified signal, perturbation, and model conditions, adversarially trained Vision Transformers can overfit while still generalizing robustly.

paragraphs: BokehDepth uses the relationship between defocus blur and scene depth to improve distance estimation from a single image. Existing bokeh methods can inherit artifacts from noisy depth estimates, while depth models can struggle with consistent physical scale or with textureless and distant regions. The paper treats synthetic defocus as an additional source of geometric information.

The framework has two stages. First, a physically grounded generative model creates calibrated stacks of bokeh images from one sharp image, without needing a depth map as input. A lightweight aggregation module then extracts information across those defocus variations and integrates it into a depth model's encoder. The decoder stays unchanged, allowing the added geometric cues to enter through the representation used for prediction.

Experiments report better visual bokeh fidelity than depth-dependent rendering baselines and consistent metric-depth improvements for state-of-the-art monocular models. The approach matters because the generated blur variations serve as a supervision-free geometric signal. Bokeh generation and depth estimation become connected parts of a framework in which synthetic optical variation helps inform physical distance predictions.
icml-2026-boosting-monocular-metric-dept.tldr: BokehDepth generates calibrated defocus variations from one image and uses them to improve monocular metric-depth estimation.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning asks a model to learn new categories without forgetting earlier ones. Replaying stored examples can help, but retaining them creates storage and privacy concerns. Generative replay instead creates examples of old categories with a frozen text-to-image model. This paper identifies a problem that arises when those synthetic examples are mixed with real examples of new categories.

The model can learn a domain shortcut: whether an image looks synthetic or real becomes a cue for its category, displacing the semantic features that should support classification. DREAM addresses this through subspace rectification and orthogonal projection to remove the shortcut, together with prototype regularization anchored in real data to strengthen semantic alignment. Its generator needs no additional training; the incremental classifier still undergoes learning.

Experiments on four datasets report that DREAM outperforms existing exemplar-free class-incremental methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The findings highlight that generating old examples is only part of successful replay. Learning must also prevent the difference between generated and real images from becoming an easy substitute for recognizing category content.
icml-2026-breaking-the-synthetic-real-do.tldr: DREAM improves generative replay by preventing synthetic-versus-real image differences from becoming shortcuts for category prediction.

paragraphs: CoDA-Bench evaluates whether coding agents can solve tasks that require both finding relevant data and writing code to use it. The paper argues that testing code skills and data skills separately misses an important part of real development: agents often face a large filesystem and must determine which resources belong in their solution before analysis can succeed.

The benchmark provides a Linux sandbox built around the Kaggle ecosystem, containing hundreds of datasets. Agents explore complex file hierarchies, identify useful resources, and generate code for analytical tasks. Its 1,009 tasks span 31 communities, and each task environment contains an average of 980 files. This makes resource discovery part of the evaluated work rather than assuming the appropriate input has already been selected.

The reported evaluation finds that even top-performing systems achieve only 61.1% success. The result exposes difficulty coordinating data discovery with code execution in these environments. CoDA-Bench therefore offers a way to assess the complete interaction between filesystem exploration and programming, making visible failures that isolated evaluations of either capability could miss.
icml-2026-coda-bench-can-code-agents-han.tldr: CoDA-Bench tests coding agents on joint data discovery and programming tasks, where evaluated top systems reach only 61.1% success.

paragraphs: Agents handling long tasks often summarize earlier interactions so they can continue reasoning with a manageable context. Producing those summaries takes decoding time and can delay the overall response. CoMem separates memory management from the main agent so summarization and agent inference can proceed in parallel.

Its asynchronous pipeline offsets memory processing by k steps, overlapping summary generation with ongoing inference. Because memory processing and action selection are no longer tightly synchronized, the memory model is trained through rewards to retain sufficient information for the agent's decisions. This connects compression quality to what the agent needs to do, rather than treating summary generation as an isolated operation.

The theoretical analysis supports a better efficiency-effectiveness trade-off than coupled architectures. On SWE-Bench-Verified, CoMem reports a 1.4× latency improvement over vanilla long-context solutions while retaining most of their performance. The gains also scale favorably as system throughput increases. These results support a modular design in which memory compression and agent reasoning can be optimized independently, with most task performance preserved despite asynchronous context processing.
icml-2026-comem-context-management-with-.tldr: CoMem overlaps memory summarization with agent inference, reporting a 1.4× latency improvement while preserving most performance on SWE-Bench-Verified.

paragraphs: DeepAnalyze targets data science that runs from raw data through analysis to a research report. The paper identifies predefined workflows as a constraint on existing data agents: a fixed sequence can support particular tasks but restrict the flexibility needed for more open-ended work. DeepAnalyze instead trains an agentic language model to acquire and combine the relevant capabilities.

Its training curriculum introduces capabilities progressively, following a learning trajectory inspired by human data scientists. A data-grounded trajectory synthesis framework creates the training examples used for this process. Training in real-world environments allows the model to integrate those skills across tasks ranging from answering questions about data to conducting open-ended data research.

Across 13 benchmarks, the 8-billion-parameter model outperforms workflow-based agents built on advanced proprietary language models. The reported comparison supports the value of training the agent's own data-science behavior, alongside the capabilities of its underlying model. DeepAnalyze is also fully open-sourced, making the presented system available for further work on agents that coordinate an entire data-science process.
icml-2026-deepanalyze-agentic-large-lang.tldr: DeepAnalyze trains an 8B agent through a data-science curriculum and outperforms tested proprietary-model workflow agents across 13 benchmarks.

paragraphs: Identical prompts can produce different model outputs when inference is distributed across different numbers of GPUs, even with greedy decoding. The paper traces this to floating-point arithmetic: changing the order in which partial results are combined can change the final numerical result. In reinforcement learning, differing training and rollout configurations can consequently assign different probabilities to the same behavior.

Tree-Based Invariant Kernels, or TBIK, enforce a consistent order for reductions both within and across GPUs. The authors implement custom matrix multiplication and reduction kernels in Triton and integrate them into vLLM and Fully Sharded Data Parallel training. The kernels guarantee bit-wise identical results across tensor-parallel sizes, addressing the numerical source of this parallelization mismatch.

The resulting pipelines achieve deterministic inference across the tested parallel configurations and zero probability divergence between rollout and training engines. Eliminating this source of mismatch enables the authors' claimed on-policy reinforcement learning at scale, with improved performance and faster convergence. The contribution links low-level arithmetic ordering to whether the probabilities used for learning match those that generated the training experience.
icml-2026-deterministic-inference-across.tldr: TBIK makes arithmetic reduction order invariant across tensor-parallel sizes, eliminating the resulting probability mismatch between rollout and training.

paragraphs: Language-conditioned segmentation requires selecting the image region described by a linguistic instruction. The paper identifies a failure in systems that generate candidate masks and then choose among them: good masks may already exist, yet the final choice can still mismatch the language. Its analysis attributes many such errors to semantic alignment rather than the quality of the candidate boundaries.

FlowSeg makes language participate throughout mask generation. Information moves in both directions between intermediate decoding states and language-model condition embeddings. The language guides each refinement step, while emerging visual evidence updates the representation of the condition. A lightweight boundary refinement component additionally focuses on uncertain areas without disturbing confident mask interiors.

Experiments on referring expression segmentation and reasoning segmentation report consistent improvements in language–mask alignment and state-of-the-art performance. The approach matters because it addresses the relationship between the requested meaning and the evolving visual region during construction. The reported gains support repeated interaction between visual and linguistic representations as a way to improve the final match.
icml-2026-flowseg-dynamic-semantic-guida.tldr: FlowSeg repeatedly exchanges visual and language information during mask generation to improve segmentation alignment with the requested meaning.

paragraphs: Parameterized Diffusion Policy, or PDP, aims to make the variety of behaviors produced by a diffusion policy easier to steer. The framework learns a smooth, continuous space of policy parameters in which distances reflect the semantic similarity of physical trajectories. This gives the parameter space behavioral meaning: proximity corresponds to similarity in the resulting motion.

The structured space supports smooth interpolation between known strategies and adaptation to new constraints without changing the policy's weights. The key idea is to make behavior selection accessible through this continuous representation. A policy can therefore use its learned range of trajectories as a basis for controlled adaptation, including combinations or variations beyond the strategies already known.

Experiments on complex benchmarks with multiple behavior modes, in simulation and on real robots, report significantly better adaptation than regular diffusion policy. Improvements are especially pronounced in scenarios requiring discovery of novel behaviors. The findings support organizing a diffusion policy's behavioral variation into a meaningful parameter space as a practical mechanism for steering and adaptation.
icml-2026-from-noise-to-control-paramete.tldr: PDP organizes diffusion-policy behaviors in a smooth parameter space, enabling steering and adaptation without updating policy weights.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models learn to generate sequences by reversing a corruption process. A major design choice is how that corruption changes the sequence, such as masking symbols or replacing them uniformly. Masking is widely used in practice, and this paper develops statistical theory to help explain its advantage over alternative corruption rules.

The authors derive generalization bounds and explicitly compare forward corruption kernels. Their central finding is that masking's bounds scale with effective data support rather than the entire ambient state space. In plain language, the relevant complexity tracks the portion of possible outcomes supported by the data, instead of charging for every theoretically possible state.

Further refinements incorporate concentration and sparsity in sequential data, showing how such structure can sharpen sample-complexity bounds. These are theoretical statements about learning requirements, providing an explanation for masking's empirical strength. The work matters because the corruption rule influences more than the mechanics of generation: it can also change how the amount and structure of available data enter generalization guarantees.
icml-2026-generalization-bounds-for-disc.tldr: The paper derives bounds showing how masking can exploit effective data support and sequence structure in discrete diffusion learning.

paragraphs: This paper approaches reinforcement learning through the ordering relationships behind value estimates. A value function expresses how desirable different situations or choices are. The authors recast its estimation as learning a partially ordered set, which represents ordering relationships without requiring every pair of elements to be comparable.

Their method, GCR-RL, builds a sequence of increasingly refined order structures. Each step refines the preceding structure and learns additional relationships from temporal-difference signals, which capture discrepancies used to update value estimates. The process maintains geometric coherence across the evolving structures. The authors develop both a Q-learning algorithm and an actor–critic algorithm to implement these refinements efficiently.

The paper analyzes theoretical properties and convergence rates, then evaluates the approach across a range of tasks. Experiments report significant sample-efficiency improvements and stable performance against strong baselines. The contribution is a way to organize value learning around consistent relationships across updates, connecting the structure of the learned estimates with how efficiently and stably reinforcement learning progresses.
icml-2026-geometric-coherence-learning-f.tldr: GCR-RL refines partial-order structures underlying value functions to improve reinforcement-learning sample efficiency and stability.

paragraphs: Asynchronous reinforcement learning speeds training by collecting experience in parallel, but some experience comes from older versions of the policy. This paper connects the resulting instability to task difficulty. Its analysis finds that gradient variance under staleness grows exponentially with difficulty, linking harder tasks to narrow solution spaces and sharper loss curvature.

The authors formulate how much staleness to allow as an optimization problem. The derived allocation decreases exponentially with task difficulty, with a decay rate equal to half the Hessian growth rate. GAS implements this principle using a bandit curriculum that selects difficulty by learning signal, execution-aware budgets that prevent slow tasks from bottlenecking rollouts, and a coupling rule that tightens budgets for harder tasks.

Mechanistic analysis finds that the observed region of coherent gradients follows the predicted exponential boundary. On code-generation benchmarks, GAS raises Pass@1 from 39.7% to 60.1% while reaching 2.3× the throughput of synchronous GRPO. These findings support coordinating curriculum and allowable policy lag so parallel collection remains productive without treating all task difficulties identically.
icml-2026-gradient-aware-scheduling-coup.tldr: GAS adjusts allowable policy staleness to task difficulty, improving reported code-generation performance while increasing training throughput.

paragraphs: A long, coherent reasoning trace can still end in an incorrect answer. Detectors that inspect the trace text or ordinary hidden states may latch onto superficial patterns because reasoning varies in form. Answer-agreement Representation Shaping, or ARS, instead learns representations organized around how stable the answer is under small internal changes.

ARS perturbs the embedding at the boundary of a reasoning trace and generates alternative answers. Each perturbation receives a label indicating whether its answer agrees with the original. Training brings answer-agreeing states closer together and separates states that produce disagreement. This turns automatically generated agreement information into a representation designed to expose latent instability associated with hallucination risk.

The resulting embeddings can be used with existing embedding-based detectors, and their training requires no human annotations. Experiments report consistent detection improvements and substantial gains over strong baselines. Agreement supplies the training signal, rather than a direct correctness label; the reported detection results show how that signal can nevertheless help identify risky answers.
icml-2026-harnessing-reasoning-trajector.tldr: ARS uses answer agreement under small latent perturbations to learn representations that improve hallucination detection without human training labels.

paragraphs: HELIX fills missing values in time series by improving how a network represents relationships among features. The paper argues that existing attention methods repeatedly rediscover these relationships at each layer, without persistent anchors. HELIX gives each feature a learned identity embedding that carries its intrinsic semantic properties throughout the network.

Those identities are combined with attention across time and features. Dependencies are learned end-to-end from how variables change together over time, rather than imposed through a predefined graph. This supports data whose features combine spatial locations with semantic variables, where assuming a uniform kind of spatial relationship may be inappropriate. Persistent identities give the changing attention computations a consistent reference for each feature.

In the reported evaluation, HELIX surpasses all 16 baselines on five public datasets across 21 settings. Mechanistic analysis also finds that learned identities and dependencies progressively align with underlying physical and semantic structure across layers. Together, these findings connect the persistent feature representation with a more effective use of cross-feature information for recovering missing observations.
icml-2026-helix-hybrid-encoding-with-lea.tldr: HELIX gives time-series features persistent learned identities, improving dependency modeling and missing-value recovery across the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Robustness certification asks whether a prediction is guaranteed to remain stable under adversarial input changes. Randomized smoothing provides a scalable approach for classification, but applying it to continuous-valued regression raises different challenges. This paper develops regression certificates that account for the local geometry of the prediction function, which existing acceptance-region approaches do not exploit.

The proposed certificate is centered on the smoothed model's prediction and guarantees its stability while remaining computable at test time. The authors investigate constructions that explicitly use means, variances, and gradients. Incorporating these quantities provides ways to describe how predictions behave locally, bringing information about the function itself into the certification procedure.

On the MNIST rotation task, using gradient information produces significantly tighter robustness certificates than the existing α-smoothing method. The stated gain concerns the strength of the certificate for a smoothed regression model. This demonstrates that local geometric information can improve a practical robustness guarantee, with the abstract's concrete empirical comparison established on the rotation task.
icml-2026-higher-order-certified-robustn.tldr: The paper uses local prediction geometry to certify smoothed regression models, obtaining tighter certificates with gradients on MNIST rotation.

paragraphs: LARFT addresses the difficulty language models have following precise output-length instructions. The paper argues that externally supplied length signals or objectives leave an underlying issue insufficiently addressed: the model's own representation of length. Its training framework therefore connects recognizing the length of a response with learning to produce a response of the requested length.

The method combines length-oriented reinforcement learning with hindsight length-awareness tasks. Responses generated by the current policy are repurposed into examples where the model learns to identify how long its own output actually was. This jointly trains internal length awareness and the generation policy, using the model's behavior as material for learning about the constraint it is supposed to satisfy.

Across four base models, LARFT reports an average improvement of 20.92 points over existing baselines on three length-following benchmarks. Four general-capability benchmarks show an average decline of 1.45 points. The results indicate a substantial improvement in length control alongside a comparatively small measured trade-off in broader capabilities within the reported evaluation.
icml-2026-larft-closing-the-cognition-ac.tldr: LARFT combines reinforcement learning with recognition of past output lengths to improve length instruction following across four base models.

paragraphs: RepoNavigator tackles issue localization: finding the files and functions that need modification in a large repository. The paper argues that treating this purely as retrieval can miss code execution logic, while supplying many auxiliary tools complicates agent control. Its design centers navigation on one operation: jumping to the definition of an invoked symbol.

That operation connects navigation to the program's execution structure and simplifies the actions the agent must learn to choose. RepoNavigator is trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning directly from a base pretrained model. It does not rely on distillation from closed-source systems, so the reported navigation capability is developed through the stated reinforcement-learning process.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results, with the 7B model outperforming 14B baselines and the 14B model exceeding 32B competitors. The 32B version also exceeds closed-source models such as GPT-5 on most metrics. These findings support pairing a focused, structurally meaningful tool with learned navigation behavior for repository-level localization. The comparisons concern finding relevant code, rather than establishing performance on every stage of software repair.
icml-2026-one-tool-is-enough-reinforceme.tldr: RepoNavigator learns repository issue localization through reinforcement learning with a single tool that jumps to invoked symbols' definitions.

paragraphs: Q-Evolve addresses credit assignment in agents that receive rewards only after completing a long interaction. A final outcome gives limited direct guidance about which earlier actions helped. The framework jointly develops a critic that supplies feedback on individual steps and a policy that learns from those signals, keeping both within a shared data distribution.

Each iteration trains the critic on a mixture of expert demonstrations and agent-generated trajectories. A weighted Implicit Q-Learning objective stabilizes value updates in the sparse-reward setting. Advantage estimates from the learned value function then become step-wise process rewards, without environment backtracking or human annotation. Policy optimization stays close to the behavior represented in the same data used to label those rewards.

On AlfWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, Q-Evolve outperforms strong baselines in sample efficiency, robustness, and overall task performance. The results support iterative improvement in which supervision and behavior evolve together. Grounding both updates in shared data is central to the approach's attempt to improve the agent without aggravating distribution shift.
icml-2026-self-evolving-llm-agents-with-.tldr: Q-Evolve jointly improves step-level reward supervision and agent policies through an in-distribution learning loop grounded in shared trajectory data.

paragraphs: SOLAR studies reward shaping for multiple agents learning offline from sparse rewards. Additional rewards can accelerate learning, but they can also change the underlying task, while guidance from a learned world model can amplify its errors. The paper finds shaping reliable when activation follows statistically validated learning plateaus and the added reward has a potential-based form.

The framework uses inexpensive simulated rollouts from a world model to test whether learning has stalled. After detecting a plateau, it adds the discounted potential of the next state minus the potential of the current state to the original reward. Potentials adapt over time, and uncertainty-aware throttling weakens shaping in regions where the world model is unreliable.

The theoretical analysis addresses preservation of policy optimality, the effect of model error on plateau decisions, and stability of adaptation operating at two timescales. Experiments report consistent gains in stability and final performance across dataset qualities on sparse-reward offline multi-agent benchmarks. The findings emphasize jointly controlling when shaping begins, its mathematical form, and its strength under uncertainty.
icml-2026-solar-for-offline-marl-plateau.tldr: SOLAR activates potential-based reward shaping after validated learning plateaus and reduces its strength where world-model uncertainty is high.

paragraphs: GiFlow recovers missing observations in systems whose measurements vary across both space and time, such as traffic or air-quality monitoring. The paper describes two obstacles in existing approaches: repeated propagation can accumulate errors, while diffusion methods require iterative sampling and often start from Gaussian distributions unrelated to the particular problem.

GiFlow changes the starting distribution. It filters observable signals across space and time to construct a graph-informed prior that better matches the distribution of the data being reconstructed. This closer starting point simplifies the generation trajectory. A hybrid vector-field model then combines spatial attention, temporal attention, and spatiotemporal propagation to represent how reconstruction should proceed.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report that GiFlow outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods. The contribution connects the choice of a generative starting distribution with the structure already available in the observations. Using that structure both in the prior and in the learned flow allows spatial and temporal relationships to inform recovery throughout the framework.
icml-2026-spatiotemporal-imputation-with.tldr: GiFlow reconstructs missing spatiotemporal data using flow matching that starts from a graph-informed prior derived from observed signals.

paragraphs: UniMapping treats simultaneous localization and mapping as a way to build a reusable representation for later perception tasks. A map must support more than tracking position: its features need consistent scale behavior and sufficient geometric fidelity to remain useful across observations. The framework constructs a persistent map of learned descriptors from multimodal input.

A Spatial-Aware Deformable Transformer introduces explicit geometric structure into feature extraction to ensure scale invariance. A separate Spatial Fusion strategy decouples feature aggregation from temporal sequences. Together, these components support accumulating information from multiple views in the map, making that accumulated context available for downstream perception rather than relying only on an individual observation.

Indoor and outdoor benchmark experiments show competitive SLAM performance. Downstream tasks also improve, with reported gains of 3.1% in mAP and 7.1% in mIoU. These findings support the framework's map-centered goal: maintaining a persistent representation can benefit later visual understanding as well as localization and mapping. The stated downstream gains are attributed to the accumulated multi-view context.
icml-2026-unimapping-unified-slam-framew.tldr: UniMapping builds persistent neural-descriptor maps that combine multi-view context to support competitive SLAM and improved downstream perception.

paragraphs: WF-Bench evaluates how well neural networks can represent quantum many-body wavefunctions. It does this by asking models to match target wavefunctions across several distinct regimes of strongly correlated matter, including topological states, Wigner crystals, and superconducting wavefunctions. The diversity of targets makes representational ability the central object of comparison.

The paper introduces a systematic, reproducible matching protocol and uses wavefunction fidelity as a common measure of agreement. This provides a consistent basis for comparing different neural-network wavefunction architectures. The authors apply the protocol to Psiformer and Ferminet, placing both within the same dataset-driven evaluation framework.

The analysis finds empirical scaling laws relating representability to physical system size and model choices, including the number of determinants and network depth. These laws summarize observed scaling behavior rather than asserting universal guarantees. The benchmark therefore serves two connected purposes: measuring which target states architectures can represent, and investigating how increasing particular model resources changes that ability. Both can inform the design of future wavefunction models.
icml-2026-wf-bench-a-benchmark-for-neura.tldr: WF-Bench compares neural-network wavefunctions through target matching and identifies empirical relationships between representability, system size, and model capacity.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time-series variables together can benefit from their relationships, but those dependencies may be noisy and change with the system's state. The paper observes that dense interaction can then spread spurious correlations and make representations overly similar. This motivates controlling how much information variables exchange, alongside improving the representations themselves.

MS-FLOW models cross-variable interaction as information flow with limited capacity. It replaces fully connected communication with sparse routing that keeps only a few critical dependency paths. Cross-variable signals enter under a strict communication budget, suppressing redundant links and the propagation of spurious correlations. The bottleneck makes selecting useful relationships an explicit part of the forecasting framework.

Across 12 real-world benchmarks, the method reports state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy while learning fewer, more reliable dependencies. The findings support selective interaction in the evaluated settings, especially given the paper's observation that dense communication can be unreliable under noisy, state-dependent relationships. The contribution is a practical way to restrict communication so that the connections retained provide more useful predictive information.
icml-2026-what-if-we-let-forecasting-for.tldr: MS-FLOW limits cross-variable communication to selected dependency paths, improving forecasting while learning fewer, more reliable relationships.

paragraphs: A deployed model reflects updates from pretraining, fine-tuning, and later adaptation or alignment. This paper asks how much a particular development stage contributed to the model's eventual behavior. It frames accountability through a counterfactual question: how would that behavior have changed if the updates from one stage had not occurred?

The proposed framework estimates stage effects without retraining the model. Its estimators account for the training data and important aspects of optimization, including learning-rate schedules, momentum, and weight decay. This matters because a stage's effect depends on how its updates were produced as well as on which examples were used.

The demonstrations show that these estimates can quantify stage contributions and identify stages associated with spurious correlations in image classification and text toxicity detection. Those attributions can then guide targeted follow-up interventions. The contribution is a practical model-analysis tool that connects observed behavior to parts of the development process, using estimated counterfactual effects to focus investigation and subsequent changes.
icml-2026-who-gets-credit-or-blame-attri.tldr: The framework estimates how individual training stages affect model behavior without retraining, helping locate stages associated with spurious correlations.
